summary: The West Virginia Mine Wars, from the 1912 Paint Creek strike to the 1921 Battle of Blair Mountain, when coal companies, hired Baldwin-Felts gunmen and bought sheriffs met some ten thousand armed union miners with machine guns and aerial bombs.

evidence.note: Esau scrip explained: miners' wives used as loan collateral, coerced sex with company guards
girls as young as twelve rented out to the company to pay family debts
UMW origins and the 1897 national strike stalled by non-union West Virginia mines
county sheriffs owned by mining companies and used as strikebreakers
April 1912 Paint Creek miners issue demands, strike begins
Baldwin-Felts mercenaries brought in, evictions and tent colonies follow
May 1920 Felts brothers arrive in Matewan, shootout with Hatfield and miners
Sid Hatfield gunned down by Baldwin-Felts men at the McDowell County courthouse, 1921
sheriff's planes drop pipe bombs and gas on miners; framed as a full military action
federal troops arrive in September 1921, miners disband; casualty estimates
treason and murder trials afterwards; New Deal unionization only briefly noted

notes: Primary subject is the event, so roles are empty. Covered span ends with the post-battle trials (1922, from general knowledge); the 1934-35 New Deal outcome is a short coda. Transcript garbles some dates (miners gathering in 'October'); the march was in August 1921. Sid Hatfield's birth year follows the transcript (aged 27 in 1920); some sources give 1891. United Mine Workers kept as a keyword: no org_type fits a labor union.
